prompt: A computer supplies web pages to other computers on the network. Which description is most accurate?
options: It performs a transit role because several clients use it.
It performs a client role while returning the requested pages.
It performs a switching role when it receives Ethernet frames.
It performs a server role while remaining a network endpoint.
explanation: A server supplies a service such as HTTP to clients and is also an endpoint on the network. Server and endpoint describe compatible roles, not mutually exclusive hardware categories.

whyWrong.0: Supplying an application is different from forwarding other hosts’ traffic as transit.
whyWrong.1: For this exchange, the computer supplies rather than requests the web content.
whyWrong.2: Receiving its own frames does not mean it switches transit frames between ports.

prompt: A PC must send an IP packet to a different IP network. Which function selects the next hop using the destination IP address?
options: A Layer 2 switch forwarding within one VLAN
An access point accepting a wireless association
A router consulting its IP routing table
A hub repeating the received electrical signal
explanation: Routing selects an outgoing path using the destination IP network and the routing table. A router or a Layer 3 switch with routing configured can supply this function.

whyWrong.0: Layer 2 forwarding uses MAC addresses within the local VLAN rather than selecting an IP next hop.
whyWrong.1: Wireless association establishes a client's connection to an AP; it does not by itself choose routes between IP networks.
whyWrong.3: A hub repeats signals and does not inspect an IP routing table.

prompt: A company wants a consistent wireless configuration across many access points. What is the main role of a wireless LAN controller?
options: Coordinate the configuration and operation of supported APs.
Provide each wireless client’s physical radio attachment itself.
Supply power allocation independently of the AP’s PoE switch.
Choose every client’s IP next hop as the campus core.
explanation: A wireless LAN controller provides centralized coordination for supported APs, including configuration and monitoring. The traffic-forwarding path depends on the wireless deployment; controller management does not mean every data frame follows the same path.

whyWrong.1: The AP supplies the client’s radio attachment; the controller coordinates AP operation.
whyWrong.2: The actual power source still needs sufficient per-port capability and total budget.
whyWrong.3: Controller coordination is not the same function as campus routing; forwarding depends on the deployment.

prompt: What is the main purpose of the core in a three-tier campus design?
options: Connect individual users and APs to the campus.
Provide transport between distribution blocks.
Combine the roles of distribution and access.
Connect each leaf to every other leaf directly.
explanation: The core interconnects distribution blocks and provides a reliable transport path across the campus. Access connects endpoints; distribution aggregates access and commonly provides routing or policy boundaries.

whyWrong.0: Direct endpoint attachment is the access layer’s main function.
whyWrong.2: A separate core interconnects distribution blocks; it is not the combined access/distribution layer described here.
whyWrong.3: That is not the core’s role in the stated hierarchical campus design.

prompt: A hosted application automatically adds capacity as demand grows and releases it when demand falls. Which cloud characteristic does this illustrate?
options: Rapid elasticity
Resource pooling
Broad network access
Measured service
explanation: Rapid elasticity is the ability to expand and reduce provisioned resources in response to demand. It differs from simply hosting a server in someone else's building.

whyWrong.1: Resource pooling concerns shared provider resources; the described change is capacity expanding and contracting.
whyWrong.2: Network access describes how the service can be reached, not this adjustment to demand.
whyWrong.3: Measured service concerns metering usage, which is different from changing provisioned capacity.

prompt: Which two statements accurately describe a next-generation firewall and an inline IPS? (Choose two.)
options: An NGFW can apply policy using identified applications.
An inline IPS can drop traffic according to its threat policy.
A stateful firewall uses only the destination IP, ignoring connection state.
An inline IPS inspects only an out-of-path traffic copy.
An NGFW’s encrypted-payload visibility is independent of decryption.
explanation: An NGFW combines traffic-policy enforcement with capabilities such as application visibility and intrusion prevention. An inline IPS sits in the traffic path and can block a detected threat, subject to its configuration and inspection capability.

whyWrong.2: Stateful inspection also uses connection-state information; this option describes too narrow a function.
whyWrong.3: Inline placement puts the IPS in the traffic path; an out-of-path copy describes a different inspection arrangement.
whyWrong.4: Encrypted content visibility depends on the traffic and available decryption, not just the NGFW label.

exhibit.title: Documented forwarding behavior — teaching evidence, not CLI output
exhibit.text:
SW3 forwards frames between local ports in each VLAN.
SW3 is configured with IP routing and serves as gateway for two IP networks.
Traffic between those networks is routed by SW3.

prompt: Which device role best matches the documented behavior of SW3?
options: A Layer 2 switch providing management access
A wireless controller managing radio settings
A hub connecting a shared Ethernet segment
A Layer 3 switch performing routing and switching
explanation: SW3 both forwards Ethernet frames within each LAN and routes between the IP networks. Those documented functions justify identifying a Layer 3 switching role; the label on a diagram alone would not establish that routing is configured.

whyWrong.0: A management IP address alone would not provide the documented forwarding between networks.
whyWrong.1: The evidence describes wired switching and IP routing, not AP management.
whyWrong.2: A hub neither learns destination MAC forwarding entries nor makes IP routing decisions.

prompt: An office adds compatible controller-managed access points on PoE switch ports. Which two statements describe the design correctly? (Choose two.)
options: The AP uses its wired uplink only for power, with no Ethernet data.
The AP connects wireless clients to the wired network through its uplink.
The controller’s budget replaces the switch’s PoE power budget.
The switch can supply power and Ethernet connectivity on the AP’s cable.
Controller management means client forwarding always bypasses the AP’s site.
explanation: The AP supplies wireless access, while a compatible PoE switch can supply both its wired connection and electrical power. A controller coordinates AP operation, but forwarding and power requirements still depend on the chosen design.

whyWrong.0: The compatible uplink carries Ethernet as well as supplying power in the stated design.
whyWrong.2: The switch’s actual source budget governs the power available on its PoE ports.
whyWrong.4: Management and forwarding are different roles; some designs switch client traffic locally.

exhibit.title: Campus design notes
exhibit.text:
Access switches connect users and APs.
Their uplinks reach a redundant pair of switches.
That pair performs both distribution and core functions.
There is no separate core layer.

prompt: Which campus architecture matches the described design?
options: A two-tier campus with a collapsed distribution/core layer
A three-tier campus because the upper layer has two switches
A spine-leaf fabric because every access switch has two uplinks
A single access layer because all switches share one site
explanation: A two-tier campus combines distribution and core functions into a collapsed layer above access. Redundant devices can exist within that layer without turning the architecture into three tiers.

whyWrong.1: Tier count follows functional layers, not the number of redundant devices.
whyWrong.2: Two uplinks alone do not establish the endpoint/leaf/spine roles of that architecture.
whyWrong.3: A site can contain several functional layers; the description explicitly gives access and combined distribution/core roles.

exhibit.title: Basic spine-leaf plan
exhibit.text:
Spines: S1, S2
Leaves: L1, L2, L3
Each leaf connects to S1 and S2.
Servers attach to leaf ports.

prompt: Which two additions fit the basic spine-leaf connection pattern in the plan? Choose two.
options: Add L4 with one link to S1 and one to S2.
Connect a new server to S1 instead of a leaf.
Attach a new server to an available L2 port.
Connect L4 only to L3, using L3 as its transit leaf.
Replace L2’s two spine links with one L1–L2 link.
explanation: A new leaf needs connectivity to each spine in the stated basic pattern, and endpoint attachment belongs on a leaf. These choices describe the physical pattern; forwarding capacity and configuration still need to be checked.

whyWrong.1: The reference pattern places endpoints on leaves, rather than directly on spines.
whyWrong.3: The new leaf would depend on another leaf instead of connecting to every spine.
whyWrong.4: Replacing the spine connections with a leaf-to-leaf path changes the stated topology.

exhibit.title: PoE allocation worksheet — supplied values
exhibit.text:
Available budget: 120 W
Existing allocations: 90 W
Remaining budget: 30 W
Each proposed AP allocation: 30 W

prompt: Each additional AP needs a 30 W allocation, and each selected port supports it. Based on the stated total budget, how many more such APs can the switch support?
options: Three additional APs
Two additional APs
No additional APs
One additional AP
explanation: The remaining allocation budget is 120 − 90 = 30 W, enough for one more 30 W AP. Per-port capability and aggregate available power must both be sufficient.

whyWrong.0: Three APs would require 90 W of additional available budget.
whyWrong.1: Two APs would require 60 W, more than the stated remainder.
whyWrong.2: The given 30 W remainder does fit one compatible 30 W allocation.

prompt: On a home device combining routing, switching and an AP, wired clients still reach the Internet. Nearby wireless clients cannot find the configured network name. Which function should be investigated first?
options: The WAN routing function that the wired clients are using
The wireless access-point function and its radio configuration
The Ethernet switching function serving the wired clients
The remote Internet server used by both kinds of client
explanation: The symptom is failure to discover the wireless network, while the wired forwarding path works. Start with the AP's radio, network-name settings and wireless environment before changing a working wired path.

whyWrong.0: Successful wired Internet use is evidence that the WAN path is working for those clients.
whyWrong.2: The failed step is wireless discovery rather than the wired clients' Ethernet attachment.
whyWrong.3: Clients must first discover and join the local wireless network before reaching a remote server.

prompt: Three branches reach headquarters through separate WAN links. Each branch's only path to the others passes through headquarters. What is the effect of losing the headquarters transit function?
options: Branch-A loses local switching as well as its WAN path.
The branches retain communication through their local gateways alone.
Communication between branches loses its only designed path.
Only requests addressed to HQ itself are affected.
explanation: In this hub-and-spoke design, interbranch communication depends on the hub's transit role. A failure there removes that path even if each branch's local LAN continues operating.

whyWrong.0: An HQ transit failure does not by itself stop switching within Branch-A.
whyWrong.1: The local gateways do not create an alternative interbranch connection.
whyWrong.3: Traffic using HQ as transit is affected even when HQ is not its final destination.

exhibit.title: Office test record — supplied evidence
exhibit.text:
PC-A and Server-A: same local subnet, different addresses
PC-A → Server-A ping: replies received
PC-A → Server-A new HTTP request: no service response
Server-A Services → HTTP: Off

prompt: Which change directly addresses the confirmed cause while preserving the working path?
options: Assign a management IP address to the switch.
Enable HTTP on Server-A, then repeat the fresh request.
Give PC-A a default gateway for this local destination.
Move Server-A to a different subnet before testing.
explanation: The actual server setting shows that HTTP is stopped. Enabling the service and retesting addresses that confirmed cause; ping already provides evidence that the same client can exchange ICMP with the server.

whyWrong.0: Local switching and the working ping do not require a switch management address.
whyWrong.2: The server is in the client’s connected subnet, so a default gateway is not needed for this exchange.
whyWrong.3: Changing the subnet adds a different requirement without starting the stopped service.
